title: Switch firmware upgrade (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade the operating system on any Cisco (IOS-XE / IOS) or Aruba (AOS-CX) switch or stack
When to useScheduled firmware upgrade, security advisory, or bug fix needing a newer release
OutageYes: the switch reboots, so connected users, phones and APs drop. Book a maintenance window

Process (same for every switch)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported for the model, for best practice and security. Cisco: prefer the suggested (gold star) release. Aruba: prefer the recommended release on the support portal. Read the release notes for the upgrade path.

  2. Approve: change approval and a maintenance window.

  3. Record the current state: version, stack members, port status, neighbours, spanning tree, PoE.

  4. Back up the config off the box (see the backup SOP).

  5. Check the image: compare its hash with the published one (e.g. sha256sum <file> on the server) before loading it.

  6. Load the image to the switch.

  7. Boot the new image and wait. Don't power off during the first boot.

  8. Check it worked against the records from step 3.

  9. Roll back to the old image if checks fail.

Commands by vendor

StepCisco IOS-XE (Catalyst 9000)Aruba AOS-CX (6000 / 6300 / 8000 series)
Current versionshow versionshow version, show images (primary and secondary slots)
Stack membersshow switchshow vsf (VSF stack) or show vsx status (VSX pair)
Free spaceinstall remove inactive, then dir flash:Not needed: images go into fixed slots
Load imagecopy <url>/cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin flash:copy tftp://<server-ip>/<image>.swi secondary (load into the slot not currently booted)
Verify on switchverify /md5 flash:<image>show images (check the version in that slot)
Boot new imageinstall add file flash:<image> activate commitboot system secondary
Checkshow version, show switch, show interfaces status, show cdp neighborsshow version, show vsf, show interface brief, show lldp neighbor-info
Roll backinstall rollback to id <id>boot system primary (the old image is still there)

Notes

  • Aruba keeps two image slots. Always load the new image into the slot you're not booted from, so the old one stays as the rollback.

  • Aruba VSX pairs: vsx update-software upgrades one switch at a time, so the pair stays up.

  • Older platforms have different syntax: Cisco classic IOS (e.g. 2960-X) and ArubaOS-Switch (e.g. 2930F). Check the model's guide.

  • If the image comes from the internal repository, check the switch can reach the cache first (see the ISR SOP).

  • Model-specific detail: see the Catalyst SOP further down this section.

title: Router firmware upgrade (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade the operating system on any Cisco router (IOS-XE / IOS) or Aruba gateway (ArubaOS / AOS 10)
When to useScheduled firmware upgrade, security advisory, or bug fix needing a newer release
OutageYes: the router reboots, so the site loses WAN and internet access. Book a maintenance window

Aruba doesn't make traditional routers. Its routing devices are gateways (branch and mobility gateways, managed by CLI or Aruba Central) and EdgeConnect SD-WAN appliances (managed by Orchestrator).

Process (same for every router)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported for the model, for best practice and security. Cisco: prefer the suggested (gold star) release. Aruba: prefer the recommended release. Read the release notes for the upgrade path.

  2. Approve: change approval and a maintenance window. Tell the site: WAN and internet go down during the reboot.

  3. Record the current state: version, interfaces, routing table size, routing neighbours, VPN tunnels.

  4. Back up the config off the box.

  5. Plan remote access: if the upgrade fails you may lose remote access to the site. Have someone on site, or console access, ready.

  6. Check the image: compare its hash with the published one before loading it.

  7. Load the image to the router.

  8. Boot the new image and wait.

  9. Check it worked against the records from step 3.

  10. Roll back to the old image if checks fail.

Commands by vendor

StepCisco IOS-XE (ISR 4000, Catalyst 8000)Aruba gateway (ArubaOS 8 / AOS 10 CLI)
Current versionshow version (also shows INSTALL or BUNDLE mode)show image version, show boot (which partition it booted from)
Free spacedir bootflash:Not needed: images go into partition 0 or 1
Test reach to the image serverping <server-ip> source <source-interface>ping <server-ip>
Load imagecopy <url>/<image>.SPA.bin bootflash:copy tftp: <server-ip> <image> system: partition <n> (the partition not currently booted)
Verify on routerverify /md5 bootflash:<image>show image version (check that partition's version)
Boot new imageInstall mode: install add file bootflash:<image> activate commit. Bundle mode: boot system flash bootflash:<image>, write memory, reloadboot system partition <n>, write memory, reload
Checkshow version, show ip interface brief, show ip route summary, routing neighboursshow image version, show ip interface brief, show ip route
Roll backInstall mode: install rollback to id <id>. Bundle: point boot system back and reloadboot system partition <old>, write memory, reload

Other ways to upgrade

  • Aruba gateways managed by Aruba Central: upgrade from Central's firmware page, not the CLI.

  • Aruba EdgeConnect: upgrade from Orchestrator (software upgrade page), not the CLI.

Notes

  • Aruba gateways keep two partitions, like Aruba switches keep two image slots. Load the new image into the partition you're not booted from.

  • Older Cisco routers (e.g. ISR G2 on classic IOS) have no install mode. Use the bundle mode steps.

  • If the image comes from the internal repository through the cache, check the source interface first (see the ISR SOP below).

  • Model-specific detail: see the ISR SOP below.

title: Wireless AP firmware upgrade (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade firmware on Cisco or Aruba access points
When to useScheduled upgrade, security advisory, or bug fix. Also happens automatically when the controller is upgraded
OutageYes: each AP reboots, so clients on it drop for a few minutes. Book a window, or use a rolling upgrade

Key idea: most APs don't get upgraded one by one. They take their firmware from whatever manages them:

How the AP is managedWhere its firmware comes from
Cisco AP joined to a Catalyst 9800 WLCThe WLC. The AP downloads the image matching the WLC version when it joins
Aruba AP on a Mobility Controller (ArubaOS 8)The controller, same idea as Cisco
Aruba AP managed by Aruba Central (AOS 10 / Instant)Aruba Central's firmware page

Process (same for every AP)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported for the controller or platform, for best practice and security. Check that every AP model on site is supported by it.

  2. Approve: change approval and a window. Tell the site Wi-Fi will drop briefly.

  3. Record the current state: AP count up, clients connected, AP versions.

  4. Pre-download the image to the APs while they're still serving clients, so the outage is only the reboot.

  5. Activate: APs reboot onto the new image, in groups if a rolling upgrade is available.

  6. Check it worked: same AP count up, clients back, SSIDs broadcasting.

  7. Roll back if needed by going back to the previous controller or platform version.

Commands by vendor

StepCisco (9800 WLC)Aruba (Central)Aruba (Mobility Controller)
AP list and versionsshow ap summary, show ap imageDevices → Access Pointsshow ap database, show ap image version
Pre-downloadap image predownload (after adding the new WLC image)Scheduled in the firmware upgradeController preloads when the upgrade is set with preload
UpgradeUpgrade the WLC (install mode). Rolling AP upgrade is available on recent releasesFirmware Management → Access Points → choose group, version, scheduleUpgrade the controller; APs follow
Checkshow ap summary (all APs Registered), show wireless client summaryAP status Up, firmware columnshow ap database (all Up)

Notes

  • Do the controller and its APs together. A version mismatch stops APs joining.

  • New AP models may need a newer controller release. Check before buying or installing new models.

  • Upgrade a small test group first on large sites, then the rest.

title: Wireless controller firmware upgrade (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade a Cisco Catalyst 9800 WLC or an Aruba Mobility Controller (and the APs that follow it)
When to useScheduled upgrade, security advisory, bug fix, or support for new AP models
OutageYes: the controller reloads and every AP on it reboots. Wi-Fi drops site-wide unless using an HA pair or rolling AP upgrade

Process (same for every controller)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported (Cisco gold star / Aruba recommended). Check every AP model on it is supported, and the upgrade path in the release notes.

  2. Approve: change approval and a window. Tell sites Wi-Fi will drop.

  3. Record the current state: version, AP count joined, client count, HA status.

  4. Back up the config off the box (see the controller backup SOP).

  5. Load the image and check its hash.

  6. Pre-download the AP image so APs only need to reboot.

  7. Activate the new image. The controller reloads, then APs rejoin on the new version.

  8. Check it worked: same AP and client counts as step 3, HA pair in sync.

  9. Roll back to the old image if checks fail.

Commands by vendor

StepCisco Catalyst 9800 (IOS-XE)Aruba Mobility Controller (ArubaOS 8)
Current stateshow version, show ap summary, show wireless client summary, show redundancyshow image version, show ap database, show user-table, show switches
Load imagecopy <url>/C9800-<platform>-universalk9_wlc.<version>.SPA.bin bootflash:copy tftp: <server-ip> <image> system: partition <n> (the partition not booted)
Verifyverify /md5 bootflash:<image>show image version
Add + pre-downloadinstall add file bootflash:<image>, then ap image predownloadSet AP image preload before reload (if supported by the release)
Activateinstall activate, then install commit after checksboot system partition <n>, write memory, reload
Roll backBefore commit: install abort. After: install rollback to id <id>boot system partition <old>, write memory, reload

Notes

  • HA pairs: Cisco 9800 SSO pairs upgrade together; check show redundancy shows both units in sync after. Aruba clusters can do a live upgrade one controller at a time if configured.

  • Aruba Mobility Conductor setups: upgrade the Conductor first, then the managed controllers.

  • Aruba AOS 10 gateways managed by Central: upgrade from Central's firmware page instead.

title: Firewall firmware upgrade (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade a Cisco ASA or Cisco Secure Firewall (FTD) appliance, single or HA pair
When to useScheduled upgrade or security advisory. Firewalls are internet-facing, so advisories are urgent
OutageSingle unit: yes, traffic stops during the reload. HA pair: near zero if done one unit at a time

Aruba has no standalone firewall. Firewalling is built into Aruba gateways and EdgeConnect. Upgrade those with the router or SD-WAN SOPs.

Process (same for every firewall)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported (Cisco gold star). Check the upgrade path; FTD often needs in-between versions.

  2. Approve: change approval and a window.

  3. Record the current state: version, HA status, VPN tunnels up, interface and connection counts.

  4. Back up the config (see the firewall backup SOP).

  5. Load the image and check its hash.

  6. HA pair: upgrade the standby first, fail over to it, then upgrade the other unit.

  7. Check it worked: VPNs up, traffic passing, HA back in sync.

  8. Roll back to the old image if checks fail.

Commands by platform

StepCisco ASA (CLI)Cisco FTD managed by FMC
Current stateshow version, show failover, show vpn-sessiondb summaryFMC: Devices → Device Management (version, HA status)
Load imagecopy <url>/asa<version>.bin disk0: (and the matching ASDM image)FMC: System → Product Upgrades → upload the package
Verifyverify /md5 disk0:<image>FMC readiness check on each device
Set boot imageno boot system disk0:/<old>, boot system disk0:/<new>, asdm image disk0:/<asdm-image>, write memory—
UpgradeSingle: reload. HA: failover reload-standby, then no failover active on the active unit, then reload that unitUpgrade FMC first (FMC must be the same or newer than its devices). Deploy pending changes, then run the device upgrade; HA pairs upgrade one unit at a time
Checkshow version, show failover, show vpn-sessiondb summaryFMC device health, HA status
Roll backPoint boot system back to the old image, write memory, reloadFMC: revert upgrade (if offered for that version), or reimage

Notes

  • FTD managed locally by FDM (no FMC): upgrade from Device → Updates in the FDM web page.

  • Keep the old image on disk until the new one is proven.

title: NAC upgrade (Cisco ISE or Aruba ClearPass)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade or patch a network access control (NAC) deployment: Cisco ISE or Aruba ClearPass
When to useScheduled upgrade, security advisory, or a patch for a known bug
OutageDepends on design. With two or more policy nodes and devices pointing at both, authentication keeps working while nodes upgrade one at a time. A single node means no 802.1X, MAB or guest logins until it's back

Process (same for both)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported (Cisco gold star / Aruba recommended). Check the upgrade path and that the hardware or VM size is supported.

  2. Approve: change approval and a window. Warn the service desk: users may fail to log on to wired or wireless during it.

  3. Record the current state: version, node list and roles, authentications per minute, recent failures.

  4. Back up config and certificates (see the NAC backup SOP).

  5. Run the readiness check the vendor provides.

  6. Upgrade in order: the primary admin node first (ISE) or the publisher first (ClearPass), then the other nodes one at a time.

  7. Check it worked: all nodes on the new version and in sync, authentications succeeding (wired 802.1X, wireless, guest).

  8. Roll back by restoring the backup onto the old version if checks fail.

Steps by product

StepCisco ISEAruba ClearPass
Current stateAdministration → System → Deployment (nodes, roles, version)Administration → Server Manager → Server Configuration
PatchAdministration → System → Maintenance → Patch Management → InstallAdministration → Agents and Software Updates → Software Updates → install the cumulative patch
Readiness checkUpgrade readiness check in the upgrade page (or the Upgrade Readiness Tool)Pre-upgrade checks in the Software Updates page
UpgradeAdministration → System → Upgrade: full upgrade or split (node-by-node) upgradeSoftware Updates → upgrade image: publisher first, then each subscriber
CheckDeployment page (all nodes Connected, in sync), Operations → RADIUS → Live LogsCluster status, Monitoring → Access Tracker

Notes

  • Switches, WLCs and gateways should list at least two RADIUS servers, so one node can be upgraded while the other serves.

  • Check the RADIUS live logs straight after each node comes back. Failures show up there first.

  • Licences and support contracts must cover the new version before you start.

title: Management platform upgrade (Cisco Catalyst Center or Aruba Central)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade the platform that manages the network: Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center, on-premises) or Aruba Central (cloud)
When to useScheduled upgrade, security advisory, or to support new device models and software
OutageNo network outage: devices keep forwarding traffic. The management tools are unavailable during a Catalyst Center upgrade

Key difference

Cisco Catalyst CenterAruba Central
Where it runsOn-premises appliance or cluster (1 or 3 nodes)Cloud (SaaS), run by HPE
Who upgrades itYouHPE, automatically
Your jobPlan and run the upgradeRead release notes, check nothing you rely on changes, keep device firmware compliant

Process: Cisco Catalyst Center

  1. Choose the release: latest supported. Check the upgrade path and that every managed device model and software version is still supported.

  2. Approve: change approval and a window. No scheduled provisioning or device upgrades during it.

  3. Back up first (see the management platform backup SOP).

  4. Check health: System → System Health all green; no failed tasks.

  5. Download: System → Software Management → download the new release.

  6. Install: system update first, then the application packages. A 3-node cluster updates each node in turn.

  7. Check it worked: System Health green, devices reachable and managed, inventory sync and Assurance data flowing.

Process: Aruba Central

  1. Watch the release notes HPE publishes for each Central update.

  2. Check the impact: new defaults, removed features, API changes that affect scripts or integrations.

  3. After the update: check devices are Up, groups and templates unchanged, alerts working.

  4. Firmware compliance: set the recommended firmware per device type in Central so devices stay on supported versions.

Notes

  • Catalyst Center upgrades can take hours. Book a long window.

  • Aruba AirWave (older, on-premises) is upgraded like Catalyst Center: back up, then install the new version.

title: SD-WAN edge upgrade (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN or Aruba EdgeConnect)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade SD-WAN edge devices (and their controllers) from the central manager, not device by device
When to useScheduled upgrade, security advisory, or bug fix
OutageEach edge reboots, so its site loses WAN briefly. Sites with two edges (HA) stay up if upgraded one at a time

Key idea: SD-WAN edges are upgraded from the manager: Cisco SD-WAN Manager (vManage) or Aruba Orchestrator. The controllers must be on the same or a newer version than the edges, so they go first.

Process (same for both)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported (Cisco gold star / Aruba recommended). Check the controller/edge compatibility matrix.

  2. Approve: change approval and a window per site. Tell sites the WAN drops briefly.

  3. Record the current state: versions, tunnels/BFD sessions up per site, control connections.

  4. Back up the manager (see the management platform backup SOP).

  5. Upgrade the controllers first, in the vendor's order.

  6. Upload the edge image to the manager.

  7. Upgrade a pilot site, check it, then the rest in batches. HA sites: one edge at a time.

  8. Check it worked: control connections and tunnels back up, traffic flowing, no alarms.

  9. Roll back to the previous version if checks fail.

Steps by product

StepCisco Catalyst SD-WANAruba EdgeConnect
Controller orderManager (vManage) → Validator (vBond) → Controller (vSmart) → edgesOrchestrator (on-premises; HPE upgrades the cloud one) → edges
Upload imageMaintenance → Software RepositoryOrchestrator: Maintenance → Software Versions
Upgrade edgesMaintenance → Software Upgrade → select devices → Upgrade (activate and reboot)Orchestrator: Maintenance → upgrade appliances → select, install and reboot
Make it permanentSet the new version as default after checksAppliance boots the new partition; old one stays for rollback
Check (CLI)show sdwan control connections, show sdwan bfd sessions, show sdwan omp peersOrchestrator: appliance status, Tunnels / Health map
Roll backActivate the previous version (edges also roll back on their own if they can't reach the controllers after the upgrade)Boot the other partition from Orchestrator

Notes

  • Never upgrade edges to a version newer than the controllers.

  • Batch by region or site type, so a bad release doesn't hit every site at once.

title: UPS / PDU firmware upgrade (any vendor)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade firmware on a UPS network management card, the UPS itself, or a managed rack PDU (e.g. APC/Schneider, Eaton, Vertiv)
When to useSecurity advisory (these cards are network devices with web pages and SNMP), bug fix, or new features
OutageNetwork card or PDU controller: no power loss, only its management page and alerts drop while it reboots. UPS firmware itself: may need the UPS in bypass. Follow the vendor's steps

Key idea: there are usually two separate firmwares. The network management card (web page, SNMP, email alerts) is safe to upgrade live. The UPS or PDU unit firmware controls the power path and carries more risk.

Process (same for every vendor)

  1. Choose the release: latest supported for the exact card and unit model. Read the release notes; some need an in-between version.

  2. Approve: change approval. For UPS unit firmware, book a window and check the load can be on bypass (unprotected) for a short time.

  3. Record the current state: firmware versions, load %, runtime, battery health, alert settings.

  4. Back up the card's config (most cards can export a config file).

  5. Upload the firmware through the card's web page, or the vendor's upgrade utility.

  6. Wait for the card to reboot. Don't power-cycle it during the upgrade.

  7. Check it worked: new version shown, settings kept, alerts and SNMP polling working, load and runtime unchanged.

Where to find it (typical)

VendorCardUpgrade from
APC / SchneiderNetwork Management Card (NMC 2/3)Web page: Configuration → Firmware Upgrade, or the NMC Firmware Upgrade Utility
EatonNetwork-M2 / Network-M3Web page: Maintenance → Firmware
VertivRDU / IS-UNITY cardWeb page: firmware or system upgrade page

Notes

  • Managed PDUs normally keep outlets on during a controller firmware upgrade. Confirm this in the release notes before upgrading a PDU feeding live equipment.

  • Change default passwords and turn off unused services (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, SNMPv1) while you're there.

title: IOS-XE upgrade on an ISR via the caching server
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade IOS-XE on an ISR 4300, downloading the image from the internal repository through the regional caching server (CACHE-SRV)
When to useScheduled firmware upgrade, security advisory, or bug fix needing a newer release
OutageYes: the router reloads. Book a maintenance window

Before you start

  1. Choose the release: the latest supported release for the model, for best practice and security. On Cisco's download page, prefer the suggested (gold star) release. Check the release notes for the upgrade path and open security advisories. Then get change approval and a maintenance window.

  2. Record the current state: show version (release, install or bundle mode), show ip interface brief, show ip route summary, routing neighbours.

  3. Check free space: dir bootflash:. Free space must be larger than the image. Remove old unused images if needed.

  4. Back up the config: copy running-config startup-config, then copy it to the backup server.

  5. Check the download source interface: show run | include source-interface. Look for ip http client source-interface.

  6. Test reach to the cache with that source: ping <CACHE-SRV-IP> source <source-interface>. If it fails, fix this first (see Troubleshooting below).

  7. Get the image's published MD5 hash.

Steps

  1. Download the image:

    • copy http://repo.example.internal/firmware/isr4300-universalk9.<version>.SPA.bin bootflash:

    • The request goes to the repository URL, but CACHE-SRV answers it if it holds a local copy. This is invisible at the CLI.

  2. Verify the file: verify /md5 bootflash:isr4300-universalk9.<version>.SPA.bin. It must match the published hash.

  3. Install. Check the mode from show version:

    • Install mode: install add file bootflash:isr4300-universalk9.<version>.SPA.bin activate commit. Answer yes to the reload prompt.

    • Bundle mode: no boot system, then boot system flash bootflash:isr4300-universalk9.<version>.SPA.bin, then write memory, then reload.

Check it worked

  • show version shows the new release.

  • Install mode: show install summary shows the new package as committed.

  • Interfaces, routes and neighbours match the pre-check records.

  • Services on the site work (users, phones, internet).

Roll back

  • Install mode: show install rollback to list rollback points, then install rollback to id <id>.

  • Bundle mode: point boot system back to the old image, write memory, reload.

  • Keep the old image on bootflash until the new one is proven stable.

Troubleshooting the download

SymptomLikely causeFix
Copy times out or failsSource IP's subnet has no route or permit to CACHE-SRV (e.g. Loopback0 in VLAN X)ping <CACHE-SRV-IP> source <int> to confirm. Set ip http client source-interface to an interface that has access, or get the subnet added
Download is much faster than expectedServed from CACHE-SRVNormal. Still check the MD5
MD5 mismatch or wrong versionStale or corrupt copy on the cacheDelete the file, retry once, then raise it with the team that runs the cache

Notes

  • Check the source interface before blaming a bad file or a dead cache. From the CLI they all look the same.

  • Background: CCNA vs Real World entries "Regional Caching Redirect" and "Cache Server Unreachable When Sourced from Loopback0".

title: Cisco IMC (CIMC) firmware update on a UCS server
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpdate CIMC, BIOS, adapter and storage firmware on a UCS C-Series server or E-Series module, using the Host Upgrade Utility (HUU)
When to useScheduled firmware upgrade, security advisory, or a new OS version that needs newer firmware
OutageYes: the server reboots, so everything running on it goes down. CIMC-only updates restart CIMC but not the host

Before you start

  1. Choose the release: the latest supported HUU for the exact server model, for best practice and security. Prefer Cisco's suggested (gold star) release.

  2. Read the release notes for the upgrade path. Some older versions need an in-between version first.

  3. Record current versions: Admin → Firmware Management in the CIMC web page, or show version over SSH.

  4. Get change approval and a maintenance window. Tell the owners of services running on the server.

  5. Shut down the OS or VMs on the server cleanly.

Steps (HUU, recommended)

  1. Download the HUU ISO for the model from Cisco. Check its MD5 against the published hash.

  2. Log in to the CIMC web page and open Launch KVM.

  3. In the KVM, attach the ISO under Virtual Media.

  4. Power-cycle the server. Press F6 for the boot menu and choose the virtual DVD.

  5. In the HUU, choose Update All. Wait for it to finish, then let it reboot.

Newer CIMC releases can run the HUU from the web page with no KVM. Look under Admin → Firmware Management.

Steps (CIMC only, via SSH)

Use only if the release notes say the new CIMC works with the current BIOS.

  1. scope cimc

  2. scope firmware

  3. update tftp <tftp-server-ip> <path>/<cimc-image>.bin

  4. activate (CIMC restarts; the host keeps running)

Check it worked

  • Admin → Firmware Management shows the new CIMC, BIOS and adapter versions.

  • Chassis → Faults and Logs shows no new faults.

  • The OS boots and its services work.

Roll back

  • CIMC keeps a backup image. Under Admin → Firmware Management, activate the backup image to go back.

  • For BIOS and adapters, run the HUU for the previous release.

Notes

  • Keep CIMC and BIOS on versions released together. The HUU does this for you.

  • E-Series in an ISR: reach CIMC from the router with ucse subslot <slot> session imc.

title: Cisco Catalyst switch IOS-XE upgrade (single switch or stack)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeUpgrade IOS-XE on a Catalyst 9000 switch or stack, using install mode
When to useScheduled firmware upgrade, security advisory, or bug fix needing a newer release
OutageYes: every switch in the stack reloads, so all connected users, phones and APs drop. Book a maintenance window

Before you start

  1. Choose the release: the latest supported release for the model, for best practice and security. Prefer Cisco's suggested (gold star) release. Check the release notes for the upgrade path and open security advisories.

  2. Get change approval and a maintenance window.

  3. Record the current state:

    • show version (release, and install mode should say INSTALL)

    • show switch (stack members, roles, all Ready)

    • show interfaces status, show cdp neighbors, show spanning-tree summary, show power inline

  4. Free up space: install remove inactive deletes old unused packages. Then dir flash: to check free space is larger than the image.

  5. Back up the config: copy running-config startup-config, then copy it to the backup server.

  6. If downloading from the internal repository, check the source interface and test reach to the cache first: ping <CACHE-SRV-IP> source <source-interface> (see the ISR SOP).

  7. Get the image's published MD5 hash.

Steps

  1. Download the image to the active switch:

    • copy http://repo.example.internal/firmware/cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin flash:

  2. Verify the file: verify /md5 flash:cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin. It must match the published hash.

  3. Install. Choose one:

    • One step: install add file flash:cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin activate commit. Answer yes to the reload prompt. The install copies the image to every stack member.

    • Safer, with auto-rollback: install add file flash:cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin activate, run the checks below, then install commit. If you don't commit before the auto-abort timer runs out, the switch rolls back to the old release on its own.

  4. Wait. The first boot can take longer if it also updates ROMMON or other low-level firmware. Do not power off the switch during this.

Check it worked

  • show version shows the new release on every member.

  • show switch shows all members Ready, same roles as before.

  • show install summary shows the new package as committed (after install commit if you used the safer option).

  • Interfaces, CDP neighbours, spanning tree and PoE match the pre-check records.

  • Users, phones and APs are back online.

Roll back

  • Not yet committed: install abort.

  • Already committed: show install rollback to list rollback points, then install rollback to id <id>.

Notes

  • Every member of a stack must run the same release. Turn on software auto-upgrade enable so a new or replacement member is upgraded to match when it joins.

  • Older Catalyst switches (e.g. 2960-X) run classic IOS, not IOS-XE, and have no install mode. On those: copy the .bin to flash:, verify the MD5, boot system flash:<image>.bin, write memory, reload.

  • Check the source interface before blaming a bad file or a dead cache, same as the ISR SOP.

title: Switch config backup and restore (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeSave any Cisco or Aruba switch's config off the box, and put it back when needed
When to useBackup: before any change or upgrade, and on a schedule. Restore: a bad change, a corrupted config, or replacement hardware
OutageBackup: none. Restore: possible, depending on the method

Process (same for every switch)

  1. Save the running config to startup.

  2. Snapshot on the device before a change.

  3. Copy off the box with SCP/SFTP where possible (TFTP is unencrypted). Name files <hostname>-<YYYYMMDD>.cfg.

  4. Check the file on the server is complete.

  5. Restore by replacing the config, never by merging over it.

  6. Check the restored config matches the backup, and you can still log in.

Commands by vendor

StepCisco IOS / IOS-XEAruba AOS-CX
Savecopy running-config startup-configwrite memory
Snapshot on devicecopy running-config flash:<name>.cfgcopy running-config checkpoint <name>
List snapshotsshow archive / dir flash:show checkpoint
Copy off the boxcopy running-config scp://<user>@backup.example.internal/configs/<file>.cfgcopy running-config sftp://<user>@<server-ip>/<file>.cfg cli

  • AOS-CX creates system checkpoints automatically after config changes. Check show checkpoint before making your own.

  • Merging a file into the running config (copy <file> running-config) leaves old lines in place. Use the replace or rollback commands.

  • Replacement hardware: SSH keys, licences and (Cisco VTP) vlan.dat are not in the config. Recreate or back them up separately.

  • Interface names differ between models and vendors. A config from another model may need editing first.

  • Cisco detail: see the Cisco config backup SOP below.

When to useBefore any change or upgrade, on a schedule, or after a failure or hardware swap
OutageBackup: none. Restore: possible; a full restore reloads the router and drops the site's WAN

Process (same for every router)

  1. Save the running config.

  2. Snapshot on the device before a change.

  3. Copy off the box with SCP/SFTP where possible. Name files <hostname>-<YYYYMMDD>.cfg.

  4. Export VPN certificates and keys separately: they are not in a plain config copy.

  5. Restore by replacing the config, never by merging over it.

  6. Check interfaces, routes, NAT and VPN tunnels match the pre-change records.

Commands by vendor

StepCisco IOS-XE (ISR, Catalyst 8000)Aruba gateway (ArubaOS 8)
Savecopy running-config startup-configwrite memory
Snapshot on devicecopy running-config bootflash:<name>.cfgbackup flash (config + certificates into flashbackup.tar.gz)

Certificates and keyscrypto pki export <trustpoint> pkcs12 scp://<user>@backup.example.internal/certs/<file>.p12 password <pw>Included in backup flash

  • Aruba AOS 10 gateways managed by Central: config lives in Central groups. Back up with the management platform SOP.

  • Cisco SD-WAN or EdgeConnect routers: config lives in the manager. Back up the manager instead.

title: Cisco config backup and restore (IOS / IOS-XE)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeSave a device's config off the box, and put it back when needed
When to useBackup: before any change or upgrade, and on a schedule. Restore: a bad change, a corrupted config, or replacement hardware
OutageBackup: none. Restore: possible, depending on the method (see below)

Before you start

  1. Confirm you can reach the backup server from the device: ping <backup-server-ip> source <mgmt-interface>.

  2. Use SCP where possible. TFTP and FTP send the config, including password hashes and SNMP strings, unencrypted.

  3. Name files <hostname>-<YYYYMMDD>.cfg so they sort by device and date.

Backup steps

  1. Save the running config locally: copy running-config startup-config.

  2. Quick snapshot on the device before a change: copy running-config flash:<hostname>-<YYYYMMDD>.cfg.

  3. Copy off the box:

    • SCP: copy running-config scp://<user>@backup.example.internal/configs/<hostname>-<YYYYMMDD>.cfg

    • TFTP (if SCP isn't available): copy running-config tftp://<backup-server-ip>/<hostname>-<YYYYMMDD>.cfg

  4. Open the file on the server and check it's complete (ends with end).

Automatic backups (archive)

The archive feature saves a copy every time someone runs write memory, and on a timer:

archive
 path flash:archive/$h-
 maximum 10
 write-memory
 time-period 1440

$h = hostname. time-period is in minutes (1440 = daily). maximum only works for local flash paths. List saved copies with show archive. If the organisation uses a central backup tool, check the device is in it instead.

Restore steps

SituationMethodCommands
Undo a bad change on a live deviceReplace the running config with a saved fileconfigure replace flash:<file>.cfg list
Same, with a safety netReplace, auto-revert unless confirmedconfigure replace flash:<file>.cfg time 10, check, then configure confirm within 10 minutes (needs archive configured)
Replacement hardware or wiped deviceLoad the file as the startup config, then rebootcopy scp://<user>@backup.example.internal/configs/<file>.cfg startup-config, then reload

Do not use copy <file> running-config to restore. It merges the file into the current config instead of replacing it, so lines that should be gone stay in.

Check it worked

  • show archive config differences flash:<file>.cfg shows no unexpected differences from the backup.

  • Interfaces, VLANs, routing and neighbours match the pre-change records.

  • You can still log in over SSH.

Roll back

  • configure replace with time: don't confirm, and it reverts on its own.

  • Otherwise: configure replace back to the snapshot taken before the restore.

Notes

  • Replacement hardware: SSH keys are not stored in the config. Run crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048 after the restore, or SSH won't work.

  • Switches in VTP server or client mode keep VLANs in vlan.dat, not the config. Back up flash:vlan.dat too, or recreate the VLANs.

  • Interface names must match. A config from a different model may need editing first.

  • Licences are not in the config. Check show license summary on replacement hardware.

title: New switch install (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:

When to useNew site or comms room, extra ports, or replacing an old switch
OutageNew install: none. Replacement: yes, during the swap. Book a window

Process (same for every switch)

  1. Plan: change approval; hostname, management IP and VLANs from IPAM; rack space, power, PoE budget, uplink type.

  2. Replacement only: back up the old switch and record its port-to-VLAN map.

  3. Stage on the bench: console in, check hardware, upgrade to the latest supported release, set up the stack, apply the standard day-0 config, save and back up.

  4. Install: rack, earth, power (separate circuits for dual power supplies).

  5. Uplinks first: connect and check the uplink and management access before patching users.

  6. Patch users, then label.

  7. Check it worked, and add the switch to monitoring and backups.

  8. Update records: IPAM, diagram, asset register.

  • Cisco detail: see the Cisco access switch install SOP below.

title: New router install (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeInstall a new Cisco router or Aruba gateway at a site edge: stage on the bench, then connect WAN and LAN and cut over
When to useNew site, router refresh, or a new WAN or internet link
OutageNew site: none. Replacement: yes, the site loses WAN during cut-over. Book a window

Process (same for every router)

  1. Plan: hostname (e.g. RTR-EDGE-01), WAN details from the carrier (circuit ID, handoff type, IP / DHCP / PPPoE, gateway), LAN subnets and VLANs, routing (static, OSPF, BGP), NAT, VPNs, management access, change approval.

  2. Replacement only: back up the old router (config, certificates) and record interfaces, routes and tunnels.

  3. Stage on the bench: console in, upgrade to the latest supported release, apply the base config (hostname, SSH only, AAA, NTP, logging, SNMPv3), then interfaces, routing, NAT and VPN.

  4. Save and back up the config.

  5. On site: rack and power. Connect LAN first, check management access, then connect WAN.

  6. Test WAN: ping the carrier gateway, then an internet or head-office address sourced from the LAN interface.

  7. Check it worked: routes learned, NAT working, VPN tunnels up, users can reach apps and the internet.

  8. Monitoring and records: add to monitoring and backups, update IPAM, diagram and asset register.

  • Test from the LAN side (source <lan-interface>) so NAT and routing are checked, not just the router itself.

  • Aruba AOS 10 gateways are provisioned from Aruba Central, and SD-WAN edges from their manager (see the SD-WAN install SOP).

title: New wireless AP install (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeInstall a new Cisco or Aruba access point so it joins its controller or Aruba Central and serves clients
When to useNew coverage area, more capacity, or a site refresh
OutageNone for a new AP

Process (same for every AP)

  1. Plan: AP location from the wireless survey or heatmap; AP name (e.g. AP-BLD1-RM101); change approval.

  2. Check power: the switch port must supply enough PoE for the AP model (802.3at / PoE+ or 802.3bt / PoE++). Check the switch's PoE budget.

  3. Configure the switch port (see table): access port in the AP management VLAN, or a trunk if the AP bridges client traffic locally.

  4. Make sure the AP can find its manager: DHCP in the AP VLAN, plus controller discovery (DHCP option 43 or DNS) or internet access to Aruba Central.

  5. Pre-provision the AP by MAC or serial: name, group or tags, site.

  6. Mount and cable the AP, then let it boot. It may upgrade its firmware on first join, so give it several minutes.

  7. Check it worked: AP joined, correct name and group, SSIDs broadcasting, a test client connects.

  8. Update records: AP name, location, MAC, serial, switch port.

Commands by vendor

Switch port, local mode (tunnels to controller)Access port in AP VLAN, spanning-tree portfast—Access port in AP VLAN

  • APs won't come up without enough PoE, or they come up with radios disabled. Check show power inline (Cisco) or show power-over-ethernet (Aruba) on the switch.

  • The AP VLAN must reach the controller or the internet (for Central). Firewalls must allow CAPWAP (UDP 5246-5247, Cisco) or Aruba's ports.

  • Channel and power are set automatically (RRM on Cisco, AirMatch/ARM on Aruba). Don't set them by hand unless there's a reason.

title: Failed wireless AP replacement (any model, Cisco or Aruba)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeSwap a dead AP for a new one with the same name, settings and coverage
When to useAP down and not recovering after a power cycle, hardware fault, or RMA
OutageThe coverage area is already down; the swap restores it

Process

  1. Confirm the AP is really faulty: check switch port status, PoE (show power inline / show power-over-ethernet), and the cable. Power-cycle the port once.

  2. Record the old AP: name, group or tags, site, switch port, MAC and serial.

  3. Pre-provision the new AP with the old AP's name and group or tags (Cisco tags attach to the MAC, so assign them to the new MAC).

  4. Swap the AP on the same mount and cable. Use the same model where possible, so coverage matches.

  5. Check it worked: joined, correct name, clients connect in that area.

  6. Clean up: remove the old AP from Central or the controller inventory; raise the RMA; update records with the new MAC and serial.

Notes

  • A different model can change coverage and PoE needs. Check both before swapping.

  • Keep one or two spare APs of the common model on hand for fast swaps.

title: New SD-WAN edge install (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN or Aruba EdgeConnect)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeBring a new SD-WAN edge online at a site using zero-touch provisioning
When to useNew site, edge replacement, or adding a second edge for HA
OutageNew site: none. Replacement: yes, during the swap

Key idea: edges are set up centrally. On site you mostly plug it in; it calls home over the internet and downloads its config.

Process (same for both)

  1. Plan: site name, WAN links (type, IP or DHCP, bandwidth), LAN subnets and VLANs, hostname (e.g. RTR-EDGE-01), template or config group, change approval.

  2. Register the device by serial number so the manager expects it.

  3. Pre-stage the config: attach the template/config group and fill in the site values.

  4. On site: rack, power, connect WAN first (it needs internet or a WAN path to reach the controllers), then LAN.

  5. Onboard: the edge calls home, authenticates, and pulls its config. Approve it if the product asks.

  6. Check it worked: control connections/tunnels up, site routes learned, users can reach apps and the internet.

  7. Update records and monitoring.

Steps by product

StepCisco Catalyst SD-WANAruba EdgeConnect
RegisterAdd serial in Cisco Plug and Play (PnP) Connect, sync to SD-WAN ManagerAppliance is linked to your account in the Cloud Portal
Pre-stageAttach a device template or configuration group, enter site valuesPreconfiguration or template group, business intent overlays
OnboardDevice gets DHCP on WAN, contacts PnP, then Validator, then ManagerAppliance appears under discovered appliances in Orchestrator → approve
No DHCP on WANBootstrap config file on USB, or manual bootstrap via consoleSet WAN IP at first boot via console or the local web page
CheckManager dashboard: device reachable; CLI show sdwan control connections, show sdwan bfd sessionsOrchestrator: appliance Up, tunnels Up, Health map green

Notes

  • The WAN link must be live before the device arrives on site, or zero-touch can't work.

  • Firewalls upstream must allow the edge to reach the controllers or cloud portal.

title: New UPS / PDU install (any vendor)
html:
PartDetail
PurposeInstall a new UPS or managed rack PDU so network gear has clean, backed-up power that can be monitored
When to useNew comms room or rack, UPS replacement, or more load
OutageNew install: none. Replacement: yes, move devices across in a window (dual power supplies avoid it)

Process (same for every vendor)

  1. Plan the load: add up the watts of everything it will power. Keep the UPS under about 80% load. Check the runtime at that load is enough for the site.

  2. Plan the power: input circuit and plug type, and A/B feeds so devices with two power supplies use two different UPS or PDU feeds.

  3. Rack: UPS at the bottom of the rack (heavy). Connect the internal battery if it ships disconnected.

  4. Charge: let the batteries charge for several hours before relying on the runtime.

  5. Network card: management IP on the management VLAN, hostname (e.g. UPS-COMMS-01), change default login, NTP, SNMPv3, email alerts, syslog.

  6. Connect loads: one power supply of each dual-PSU device to feed A, the other to feed B.

  7. Shutdown agents: if servers are on it, set up the vendor's shutdown software (e.g. APC PowerChute, Eaton IPM) so they shut down cleanly before batteries run out.

  8. Test: run a self-test; check load %, runtime estimate and battery status.

  9. Monitoring and records: add to monitoring (SNMP), label, record serial, battery install date and replacement due date.

Check it worked

  • Self-test passed, battery status OK.

  • Load under 80%, runtime meets the site's need.

  • Alerts arrive in monitoring and email (test by triggering a self-test or test alert).

  • Every dual-PSU device shows both power supplies OK (show environment power on Cisco, show environment power-supply on Aruba).

Notes

  • UPS batteries usually last 3 to 5 years. Record the replacement date so it doesn't fail during an outage.

  • Don't plug laser printers or heaters into a UPS; the surge load can trip it.

title: New Cisco access switch install
html:
PartDetail
PurposeInstall a new Catalyst access switch (or stack): pre-stage on the bench, then rack, connect and hand over
When to useNew site or comms room, extra ports, or replacing an old switch
OutageNew install: none. Replacement: yes, users on the old switch drop during the swap. Book a window

Before you start

  1. Get change approval.

  2. Get the allocations from IPAM or the network team: hostname (e.g. SW-ACCESS-01), management IP, gateway, VLANs.

  3. Check the site: rack space (RU), power circuits and UPS, PoE budget for phones and APs, uplink type (fibre SFP or copper) and patching plan.

  4. Record the serial number and check the licence.

  5. Replacement only: back up the old switch's config and record its port-to-VLAN map (show interfaces status, show cdp neighbors).

Stage on the bench

  1. Console in (9600 baud, 8N1). Answer no to the initial configuration dialog.

  2. Check the hardware: show version, show inventory.

  3. Upgrade to the latest supported release (see the Catalyst upgrade SOP).

  4. Stack only: connect stack cables and power, then set the intended active switch: switch 1 priority 15. Check with show switch.

  5. Apply the standard day-0 config: hostname, SSH only, AAA, NTP, logging, SNMPv3, management VLAN and IP, VLANs, access and trunk ports, spanning tree, unused ports shut. Template: Day-0 production config.

  6. Replacement only: match the old switch's port-to-VLAN map.

  7. Save and back up: copy running-config startup-config, then copy it to the backup server (see the backup SOP).

Install on site

  1. Rack and earth the switch. Connect each power supply to a different circuit if it has two.

  2. Connect the uplinks first. Check the trunk and management before patching any users.

  3. Test from the switch: ping <gateway-ip>, then SSH in from the management network.

  4. Patch access ports to the patching plan. Replacement: move cables one-for-one from the old switch.

  5. Label the switch and uplinks.

Check it worked

  • show interfaces trunk: uplinks trunking with the right allowed VLANs and native VLAN.

  • show cdp neighbors: the upstream switch seen on the expected ports.

  • show spanning-tree summary: no unexpected blocked ports. This switch is not root.

  • show interfaces status: user ports up in the right VLANs.

  • show power inline: phones and APs powered, budget not exceeded.

  • show ntp associations: time synced.

  • Monitoring (SNMP), syslog and the backup system can see the switch.

  • Users, phones and APs work.

Roll back

  • New install: shut the uplink port on the upstream switch, fix the config over console, try again.

  • Replacement: move the cables back to the old switch (keep it racked until the new one is proven).

Notes

  • Uplinks before users: patching users onto a switch with a wrong trunk or STP setup can cause a loop or outage.

  • BPDU Guard and PortFast on access ports only, never on uplinks.

  • Update the records after: IPAM, network diagram, asset register, monitoring.

title: Cisco IMC (CIMC) management
html:
CIMC is the out-of-band management controller on Cisco UCS servers, like HPE iLO or Dell iDRAC. It works even when the server is off.

Ways in

MethodUse
Web page (HTTPS to the CIMC IP)Day-to-day work: health, KVM, power, logs
SSH command lineScripting and quick checks (scope commands)
F8 at server bootFirst-time setup, or when the CIMC IP is unknown
Redfish / XML APIAutomation and monitoring tools
From an ISR (E-Series only)ucse subslot <slot> session imc

Common tasks

TaskWhere
Remote console (screen, keyboard, mouse)Launch KVM
Mount an ISO for an OS install or HUUKVM → Virtual Media
Power on, off, cycleHost Power, or SSH: scope chassis then power cycle
Health: temperature, fans, power supplies, disksChassis → Sensors and Storage
Fault and event logsChassis → Faults and Logs (System Event Log)
Network settingsAdmin → Networking: NIC mode (dedicated or shared), IP, VLAN
Users and passwordsAdmin → User Management
AlertsAdmin → Communication Services: SNMP, syslog, email
TimeAdmin → NTP
Support bundle for Cisco TACAdmin → Utilities → Export Technical Support Data

Baseline settings

  • CIMC on the management VLAN, not a user VLAN.

  • Default admin password changed.

  • NTP and syslog set, so logs have correct times and are kept off the box.

  • SNMP or email alerts on for hardware faults.

Menu names can differ slightly between CIMC versions.
